notes: The difficult command can mean setting oppression right, correcting an oppressor, or helping the oppressed. All readings place justice at the center of the surrounding commands.
The invitation is language of settling a dispute, not simply a request for abstract reasoning. The stained cloth imagery follows it.
vocabulary: Lye
A cleansing substance used here in the refining image; the exact comparison can also be heard as thorough purification.

notes: The charge combines influences from the east, divination, and dealings with foreigners. The final hand-related expression may describe striking agreements or welcoming foreign practices.
The second object paired with Tarshish ships is uncertain: splendid vessels or desirable works or images are possible.
vocabulary: Zion
Jerusalem’s sacred hill and, by extension, the city viewed as the place of God’s instruction and rule.

sections.1: The Mountain of the LORD and the Day of the LORD

notes: The Hebrew text used here names children and women in the rebuke. Alternative readings involving oppressors or creditors are not silently substituted for that gendered language.
The last word may refer to their scalp or their private parts. The threat involves humiliating exposure, and its ambiguity is consequential.
Several ornament and garment names are uncertain. The list preserves its accumulation of costly adornments without claiming exact modern equivalents.
vocabulary: Sodom
The ruined city becomes a comparison for openly displayed wrongdoing; the line does not hide the comparison inside a general word for evil.

notes: “Growth” can also be “branch” or “sprout.” Here it is paired with the land’s fruit; the translation leaves later interpretive connections to readers.
The Hebrew word can mean “spirit,” “wind,” or “breath.” Judgment and burning remain the two linked actions.
vocabulary: Canopy
A protective covering, associated elsewhere with shelter or a bridal chamber.

sections.1: The Branch and a Purified Zion

notes: The Hebrew pairs mishpat, “justice,” with mispach, “bloodshed,” and tsedaqah, “righteousness,” with tseaqah, “outcry.” The similar sounds sharpen the failed expectations.
A “yoke” describes the land a team plows, not a fixed modern acre. The harvest is disastrously small: one bath of wine and one ephah returned from a homer of seed.
The Hebrew text used here refers to strangers or sojourners in the second line. “Lambs” there reflects a different reading.
vocabulary: Bath, homer, ephah
Ancient capacity measures. A homer is ten ephahs; the yield here is only a tenth of the seed measure.

notes: The speech shifts from “I” to “us.” The commands to dull the people’s response remain commands, without rewriting them as a prediction alone.
The tree-cutting comparison leaves a stump and calls the holy seed its stump. The image of destruction and remaining life stays compressed.
vocabulary: Seraphim
Heavenly beings whose Hebrew name is related to burning; each has six wings in this vision.

notes: The pointed Hebrew can be read as making the request deep or high. Reading the same consonants as Sheol yields “as deep as Sheol”; the draft keeps the depth image without requiring that repointing.

The Hebrew describes a young woman of marriageable age and her pregnancy or impending conception. It does not itself use the usual word specifying virginity. The naming verb addresses her as “you”; Immanuel means “God is with us.”
“Hair of the legs” can function as a euphemism for pubic hair. The shaving image threatens comprehensive humiliation.
vocabulary: Shear-jashub
Isaiah’s son’s name means “a remnant will return.” The name participates in the chapter’s signs.

notes: The Hebrew text used here speaks of rejoicing with Rezin and Remaliah’s son. Readings about melting in fear use a different understanding or alteration of the text.
The source includes both a sanctuary and a stone or rock that causes stumbling, followed by a trap. All those images are retained.
The relation of the final clause to the preceding instruction is compressed. The draft retains the image of having no dawn rather than turning it into a general verdict about ignorance.
vocabulary: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
A sign-name meaning roughly “quick spoil, speedy plunder,” explained by the coming removal of Damascus’s and Samaria’s wealth.

notes: This public verse is Hebrew 8:23; public 9:2–21 correspond to Hebrew 9:1–20.
The draft follows the reading tradition’s “for it” in the joy clause. The written form is “not,” which creates a substantially different line.

The royal names are densely joined in Hebrew, and their divisions and relation to the child are debated. The draft preserves the familiar title sequence without adding an explanation of the child’s identity.
vocabulary: Flesh of his own arm
The Hebrew text used here’s bodily image of destructive hunger; some translations read “neighbor” through a textual alteration.

notes: The final comparison is difficult and may picture a sick person wasting away or a standard-bearer collapsing.
The Hebrew says the yoke breaks because of “fatness” or “oil.” A well-fed neck outgrowing its yoke is possible; “anointing” is an interpretive explanation, not an explicit verb here.
vocabulary: A remnant will return
The words repeat the meaning of Shear-jashub’s name in 7:3, connecting the sign-name with the remnant theme.

notes: The verb is related to smelling and can express taking delight. The following lines contrast sensory appearances with just judgment.
The restored people’s conquest and dominance over their neighbors remain explicit; the animal-peace imagery is not used to remove these later lines.
vocabulary: Jesse
David’s father. A shoot from his cut-down stock evokes renewed life in that royal family.

sections.1: A Shoot from the Stump of Jesse

notes: The source uses both YAH, the short divine name, and the full name represented here by **LORD**. Both are retained.
vocabulary: Salvation
Deliverance or rescue, pictured as water drawn from wells.

notes: The text explicitly describes infants being dashed to pieces and women being raped. These harms are preserved rather than hidden in general language about disaster.
The animal names are not all securely identified. The “goat-demons” may evoke uncanny beings as well as the desolation of the ruined city.
vocabulary: Shaddai
A divine title, traditionally rendered “Almighty”; its derivation is uncertain.

notes: The rare Hebrew word is often related to extracting gold or tribute. “Fury” follows a proposed change of a consonant. “Extortion” keeps the economic sense without treating that emendation as the source text.
“Shining one, son of dawn” occurs in a taunt against Babylon’s king. The draft retains the celestial image without replacing it with the proper name Satan.
Zaphon can mean north and also name a mountain associated with divine assembly in ancient imagery.
vocabulary: Sheol
The realm of the dead, personified here as stirring to greet the fallen ruler.

notes: “The temple” may instead represent a place named Bayith. The relationship of the temple, Dibon, and the high places is compressed; the draft understands the high places as belonging to Dibon.
Eglath-shelishiyah may be a place name or mean “a three-year-old heifer.” The translation preserves it as a name while leaving that alternative visible.
vocabulary: Dimon
The name sounds like the Hebrew word for blood, intensifying the line’s mourning.

notes: The pointed Hebrew reads “my outcasts,” followed by an address to Moab. Reading “Moab’s outcasts” changes that relationship; the draft follows the pointed text.
The speaker joins Moab’s grief. The lament is preserved alongside the judgment without supplying a new speaker whenever its emotional direction changes.
vocabulary: Years of a hired worker
A carefully counted term of service; the image gives the three-year limit precision.

sections.1: Moab and the Throne of Steadfast Love

notes: The Hebrew wording names wooded or abandoned heights. “Hivite and Amorite” reflects an alternative ancient reading rather than these exact consonants.
The final harvest line is compressed and uncertain; it combines a lost harvest, grief, and incurable pain rather than explaining a farming technique.
vocabulary: Gleanings
Fruit left after harvesting, here two or three olives at the top and four or five on the branches.

notes: The nation’s physical description and the phrases about measuring or trampling are difficult. The draft keeps their ancient descriptive force without identifying a modern ethnic group.
vocabulary: Cush
A region south of Egypt in the ancient geographic horizon; it should not simply be equated with one modern country.

notes: “Foundations” may figuratively name social supports or a class of workers. The following phrase is also uncertain about the workers’ role.
The Hebrew text used here names a “City of Destruction.” “City of the Sun” is an ancient textual alternative, not the reading silently adopted here.
The final clause can describe Egypt worshiping with Assyria or serving Assyria. The shared blessing that follows favors the worship reading used here.
vocabulary: My people
God applies this designation to Egypt, calls Assyria the work of his hands, and calls Israel his inheritance; the three distinct expressions are retained.

notes: Nakedness and exposed buttocks are explicit in the sign and its explanation. The draft does not soften the predicted humiliation into merely poor clothing.
vocabulary: Commander
The Assyrian title traditionally transliterated Tartan; Sargon is the king who sends him.

sections.1: A Sign Concerning Egypt and Cush

notes: Media receives its own command to besiege. The final first-person promise about ending groaning belongs to the next clause.
The rare middle phrase may describe laying a covering or rug; an interpretation involving setting a watch is also traditional.
The Hebrew text used here has “lion.” The draft supplies “like” to express a lion-like cry; “the lookout cried” follows a different textual reading.
vocabulary: Morning and night
The watchman’s answer promises morning while still naming night; its unresolved quality is preserved.

notes: The Hebrew can suggest being bound without a bow being used, or being captured by bowmen. The draft follows the former interpretation.
The source shifts from “I” to “he” in describing removal from office. The translation retains the shift.
The peg once driven into a firm place now gives way. The draft preserves the reversal rather than harmonizing it with the earlier promise.
vocabulary: Key of David’s house
An image of entrusted authority over access, developed by the paired actions of opening and shutting.

notes: The final word literally evokes a girdle or restraint; a harbor-related interpretation is also possible. The translation keeps the image of restraint being gone.
The relation between the Chaldeans, Assyria, and the devastated land is syntactically difficult. The draft does not supply a detailed historical reconstruction to settle it.
The prostitute’s earnings become dedicated to the **LORD** and supply food and clothing for those before him. The striking economic and moral reversal remains explicit.
vocabulary: Seventy years
The stated period of Tyre’s being forgotten, compared with the days of one king; it recurs when the city is visited again.
